title: 🚀 CSR vs SSR vs SSG — What's the Difference?
excerpt: Should the page be generated in the browser, on the server for each request, or ahead of time? 🤔
body:
ㅤ
📘 Engineering Notes | From Concepts to Code — Post 08
ㅤ
When building web applications with React and Next.js, choosing how pages are rendered is an important decision.

Should the page be generated in the browser, on the server for each request, or ahead of time? 🤔

Let's understand three common rendering strategies! 👇
ㅤ
1️⃣ 𝗖𝗦𝗥 — 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁-𝗦𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 🌐

With CSR, JavaScript runs in the browser to generate or update the page content.

How it works:

1. Browser receives the initial HTML.
2. JavaScript loads and executes.
3. React renders the content.

✅ Great for interactive dashboards
✅ Useful for authenticated interfaces
✅ Supports dynamic user interactions

⚠️ Initial content may take longer to appear if it depends heavily on JavaScript.
ㅤ
2️⃣ 𝗦𝗦𝗥 — 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿-𝗦𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 🖥️

With SSR, the server generates HTML when a request is made.

How it works:

1. User requests a page.
2. Server renders the HTML.
3. Browser receives the page.
4. React can hydrate interactive components.

✅ Useful for frequently changing content
✅ Can improve initial content visibility
✅ Helpful for SEO when content is server-rendered

⚠️ Rendering can add server processing time.
ㅤ
3️⃣ 𝗦𝗦𝗚 — 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗦𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 ⚡

With SSG, HTML is generated ahead of time, usually during the build process.

How it works:

1. Pages are generated before requests.
2. Generated HTML is stored.
3. Users receive pre-rendered pages.

✅ Fast delivery through caching/CDNs
✅ Great for blogs and documentation
✅ Reduces request-time rendering work

⚠️ Content may need rebuilding or revalidation to stay fresh.
ㅤ
🔄 𝗤𝘂𝗶𝗰𝗸 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗻

🔹 CSR → Browser renders content
🔹 SSR → Server renders per request
🔹 SSG → Pages generated ahead of time
ㅤ
💡 𝗠𝘆 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆

There is no single best rendering strategy.

CSR works well for highly interactive interfaces.

SSR is useful when content needs request-time rendering.

SSG is a strong choice for content that changes less frequently.

Modern Next.js applications can combine different rendering approaches based on application requirements.

Choosing the right strategy helps improve performance, SEO, and user experience.
